author: Jessica Fern
concept: Attachment patterns have dimensions
refresher: Anxiety concerns whether others will be available; avoidance concerns discomfort with dependence and closeness. Use these dimensions to notice patterns, rather than treating a style as an unchangeable identity.
quote: Some researchers have proposed that attachment is better described using the two dimensions of attachment anxiety and attachment avoidance, and looking at the different ways these dimensions can interact.

links.title: Chris Fraley · Adult attachment theory and research

author: Jessica Fern
concept: Boundaries can protect connection
refresher: A boundary can preserve closeness while making room for personal needs. Name what you are comfortable with and listen to the other person’s limits; connection need not require abandoning yourself.
quote: Porous boundaries arise when we are connected but not protected, and rigid boundaries stem from being protected, but not connected. Healthy boundaries are when we are connected and protected.

links.title: love is respect · Understanding personal boundaries

author: Jessica Fern
concept: Consent defines consensual nonmonogamy
refresher: The defining condition is mutual knowledge and consent. Discuss what each person agrees to, rather than assuming that a shared relationship label means identical expectations.
quote: Consensual nonmonogamy is an umbrella term for the practice of simultaneously having multiple sexual or romantic partners where everyone involved is aware of and consents to the relationship structure.

links.title: Division 44 CNM Committee · What consensual nonmonogamy means

author: Jessica Fern
concept: Agree on the attachment role
refresher: Fern distinguishes having a relationship from choosing to be attachment figures. Clarify whether each person wants to offer dependable comfort and support for exploration, instead of assuming that commitment means the same thing to everyone.
quote: The antecedent to being polysecure with your partners is first getting clear about whether you want to be attachment figures for each other.

links.title: Chris Fraley · Safe havens and secure bases in adult attachment

author: Jessica Fern
concept: Make undistracted presence intentional
refresher: Reserve a mutually workable time for attention without competing screens. Presence becomes something partners can count on, rather than something squeezed between notifications.
quote: It can be helpful to have designated times of the day or during the week where you are both off your phone and focused on each other, so that the times when you are on your phone throughout the day do not become problematic.

links.title: Gottman Institute · Creating rituals of connection

author: Jessica Fern
concept: Express what makes a partner precious
refresher: Name a specific act of care and why it mattered. Expressed appreciation makes affection visible instead of asking a partner to infer it from the relationship’s existence.
quote: With your partners, take on a gratitude practice where you set aside a regular time to each appreciate the ways in which they’ve been supportive or shown up that have been meaningful to each of you.

links.title: Gottman Institute · Shared meaning and appreciation rituals

author: Jessica Fern
concept: Attunement starts with curiosity
refresher: Try to understand your partner’s experience before fixing or evaluating it. Paraphrase what you heard and ask whether you understood, leaving room for correction.
quote: Attunement is meeting your partner with curiosity, wanting to understand their feelings and needs. It is the feeling of being seen, understood and “gotten” by the other.

links.title: Greater Good in Action · Active listening

author: Jessica Fern
concept: Create dependable rituals of connection
refresher: In Fern’s framework, recurring moments together help make care predictable. Agree on a greeting, check-in, or shared activity that fits this particular relationship rather than copying someone else’s routine.
quote: Our attachment system is comforted by routine and regularity.

links.title: Gottman Institute · Examining relationship rituals

author: Jessica Fern
concept: Offer yourself the care you offer a friend
refresher: Secure relating also includes how you respond to yourself. Acknowledge a difficult moment with kindness while still taking responsibility for what needs to change.
quote: I am talking about the importance of positive self-talk and being kind and loving to yourself in ways that you would probably treat a friend, but so frequently forget when it comes to your relationship with yourself.

links.title: Kristin Neff · The elements of self-compassion

author: Michael E. Gerber
concept: Work on the business that serves your life
refresher: Step back from delivery to design how the business should operate. Judge that design against the life you want it to support, including your time and responsibilities.
quote: Once you recognize that the purpose of your life is not to serve your business, but that the primary purpose of your business is to serve your life, you can then go to work on your business, rather than in it, with a full understanding of why it is absolutely necessary for you to do so.

links.title: SBA · Planning a business

author: Michael E. Gerber
concept: Document the routine before handing it over
refresher: A process that lives only in someone’s memory makes each handoff an exception. Write down the steps, expected result, and points requiring judgment so another person can perform and improve it.
quote: Without documentation, all routinized work turns into exceptions.

links.title: GitLab · Using and maintaining a shared handbook

author: Michael E. Gerber
concept: Measure whether an innovation actually helps
refresher: Choose an outcome before changing the process. Compare results with the prior approach, then keep, adjust, or discard the change instead of equating novelty with improvement.
quote: To be at all effective, all Innovations need to be quantified. Without Quantification, how would you know whether the Innovation worked? By Quantification, I'm talking about the numbers related to the impact an Innovation makes.

links.title: ASQ · Plan, do, check, act

author: Michael E. Gerber
concept: Give each responsibility a clear owner
refresher: List the work and expected outcomes before assigning people. One person can hold several roles, but each responsibility needs a clear owner and an understood handoff.
quote: If everybody's doing everything, then who's accountable for anything?

links.title: Atlassian · Defining roles and responsibilities

author: Culadasa (John Yates), Matthew Immergut, and Jeremy Graves
concept: Focus without losing background awareness
refresher: The book distinguishes the object in focus from the wider field you can still notice. During practice, attend to the breath while allowing surrounding sensations to remain present.
quote: Conscious experience takes two different forms, attention and peripheral awareness. Whenever we focus our attention on something, it dominates our conscious experience. At the same time, however, we can be more generally aware of things in the background. Those are two ways of "knowing" the world. In meditation, we work with both attention and peripheral awareness to cultivate stable attention and mindfulness.

links.title: Greater Good · Mindfulness and awareness

author: Culadasa (John Yates), Matthew Immergut, and Jeremy Graves
concept: Reward noticing that the mind wandered
refresher: Noticing distraction is part of the practice. Recognize that moment without self-criticism, then gently return to the chosen object.
quote: A critical moment occurs during mind-wandering when you suddenly realize you're no longer observing the breath. Loosing your focus wan't something you did, it happens unconsciously. And how do you train something that happens unconsciously? Simply take a moment to enjoy and appreciate "waking up" from mind-wandering. Avoid becoming annoyed or self-critical about mind-wandering. You should positively reinforce introspective awareness.

links.title: Greater Good in Action · Returning to the breath

author: Culadasa (John Yates), Matthew Immergut, and Jeremy Graves
concept: Notice an emotion without becoming its label
refresher: Describe impatience as a present experience rather than your identity. This shift can create room to observe the feeling and choose how to respond.
quote: Impatience is an emotion. Act as you should act with all the emotions while meditating. Don't identify with it by thinking 'I am impatient'. Regard it as just one more feeling that arises and passes away, thinking 'Impatience is arising'.

links.title: Greater Good in Action · Noticing thoughts and feelings

author: Culadasa (John Yates), Matthew Immergut, and Jeremy Graves
concept: Allow background thoughts without chasing them
refresher: The aim here is not an empty mind. Let a passing thought remain in the background while returning attention to the practice, without fighting it or following its story.
quote: You aren't trying to eliminate the distractions entirely from awareness. As long as they stay in the background, let them come, let them be, and let them go.

links.title: Greater Good in Action · Mindful breathing

author: Culadasa (John Yates), Matthew Immergut, and Jeremy Graves
concept: Use walking as an attention practice
refresher: Walking offers a different anchor from seated breath practice. Notice the changing sensations of contact and movement; when attention drifts, return to those sensations.
quote: When you catch your mind wandering, simply bring yourself back to the present by focusing your attention on the sensations in your feet.

links.title: Greater Good in Action · Walking meditation

author: Ray Dalio
concept: Diagnose the cause before fixing the symptom
refresher: A recurring small failure may reveal a larger weakness in the process. Investigate what produces it before choosing a remedy, then check whether the intervention prevents recurrence.
quote: Make sure you spend enough time with the small problems to make sure they're not symptoms of larger ones.

links.title: ASQ · Root cause analysis

author: Ray Dalio
concept: Invite evidence that could change your mind
refresher: Being open-minded is an active practice: ask where your reasoning could fail and make disagreement welcome. Change your view when the evidence warrants it, rather than treating correction as a loss.
quote: To be radically open-minded, you need to be so open to the possibility that you could be wrong that you encourage others to tell you so.

links.title: John Stuart Mill · Why contrary opinions deserve a hearing

author: Ray Dalio
concept: Restate the other view before disputing it
refresher: Check whether you can explain the other person’s reasoning in terms they recognize. Correcting your understanding first makes it easier to locate the real disagreement.
quote: A good exercise to make sure that you are doing thoughtful disagreement well is to describe back to the person you are disagreeing with their own perspective.

links.title: Greater Good in Action · Active listening

author: Ray Dalio
concept: Choose goals by accepting their trade-offs
refresher: Pursuing one attractive path uses time and resources that cannot serve another. Name what you are giving up so a new opportunity does not quietly displace your actual priority.
quote: I learned that if you work hard and creatively, you can have just about anything you want, but not everything you want. Maturity is the ability to reject good alternatives in order to pursue even better ones.

links.title: Federal Reserve Education · Opportunity cost

author: Ray Dalio
concept: Judge a decision using information available then
refresher: A bad result does not automatically mean the original reasoning was poor. Reconstruct the options, probabilities and evidence available at the time before deciding what the process should change.
quote: Evaluate the merits of a past decision based not on what you know now but only on what you could have reasonably known at the time the decision was made (said by me: be aware of hindsight fallacy).

links.title: Baron and Hershey · Outcome bias (research paper, PDF)

author: Ray Dalio
concept: Make expectations explicit before judging performance
refresher: Agree on the outcome, responsibilities and standard of success before evaluating delivery. An unstated expectation is a communication gap, not evidence that someone knowingly failed their role.
quote: If you didn't make the expectation clear, you can't hold people accountable for it not being fulfilled.

links.title: Atlassian · Clarifying roles and responsibilities

author: Douglas Murray
concept: A message can lose its original audience
refresher: A post intended for one group can reach people who lack its shared history or assumptions. Recover the surrounding conversation before interpreting a fragment as a complete account of someone’s position.
quote: ‘Context collapse’: a conversation meant for an in-group becomes known to an out-group with no knowledge of the original context of the discussion.

links.title: Marwick and boyd · Context collapse (research paper, PDF)

author: Douglas Murray
concept: Attention can reward outrage
refresher: Murray highlights an incentive in online debate: strong outrage attracts attention. Research on social feedback provides a related mechanism; distinguish what becomes visible from what is representative or well supported.
quote: This is an important cog in the crowd-maddening mechanism: the person who professes themselves most aggrieved gets the most attention. Anyone who is unbothered is ignored. In an age of shouting for attention on social media the mechanism rewards outrage over sanguinity.

links.title: Brady and colleagues · Social learning and online outrage

author: Douglas Murray
concept: Hearing disagreement can clarify a belief
refresher: Mill’s argument values objections that expose errors, reveal partial truths, or keep sound beliefs from becoming unexamined slogans.
quote: Four reasons for why free speech was a necessity for a free society: the first and second being that a contrary opinion may be true, or true in part, and therefore may require to be heard in order to correct your own erroneous views; the third and fourth being that even if the contrary opinion is in error, the airing of it may help remind people of a truth and prevent its slippage into an ignorant dogma.

links.title: John Stuart Mill · On Liberty, freedom of discussion

author: Arthur C. Clarke
concept: A claim of infallibility is not a reliability test
refresher: HAL’s assurance is part of the novel’s tension between machine authority and human judgment. Treat a system’s confidence as something to evaluate against evidence, monitoring and independent checks.
quote: “I don’t want to insist on it, Dave, but I am incapable of making an error."

links.title: NIST · Evaluating and managing AI risks

author: Gabriel García Márquez
concept: Repeated patterns make time feel circular
refresher: The novel returns to names, desires and conflicts across generations. Its circular sense of time invites attention to what a family repeats, even while individual lives move toward irreversible endings.
quote: “What di you expect? Time passes”. She shuddered with the evidence that time was not passing, as she had just admitted, but that it was turning in a circle.

source.file: One hundred years of solitude notes.html

links.title: SEMO Faulkner Studies · Historical and mythical time in the novel

author: F. Scott Fitzgerald
concept: Privilege can insulate people from consequences
refresher: Nick’s judgment of Tom and Daisy links carelessness to the ability to retreat from damage. The passage asks who bears the consequences when those with protection leave others to repair the harm.
quote: They were careless people, Tom and Daisy - they smashed up things and creatures and then retreated back into their memory or their vast carelessness, or whatever it was that kept them together, and let other people clean up the mess they had made...

links.title: National Endowment for the Arts · Reading The Great Gatsby

author: Paulo Coelho
concept: Action gives a dream practical feedback
refresher: In the story, the journey teaches what wishing alone cannot. Treat a manageable action as a way to discover obstacles and revise your approach, rather than waiting for complete certainty.
quote: "There is only one way to learn," the alchemist answered. "It's through action".

links.title: ASQ · Learning through small tests and reflection

author: Paulo Coelho
concept: A fallback can make exploration possible
refresher: Santiago recognizes skills he can return to if the journey fails. A credible fallback can make an uncertain choice more manageable without guaranteeing that taking the risk will succeed.
quote: He suddenly felt tremendously happy. He could always go back to being a shepherd. He could always become a crystal salesman again.

links.title: Harvard Program on Negotiation · Evaluating your alternative

author: Atul Gawande
concept: Comfort-focused care is still active care
refresher: Hospice changes the priority toward comfort and quality of life; it is not abandonment. Palliative care can also accompany disease-directed treatment, so discuss which services fit the person’s needs and goals.
quote: The difference between standard medical care and hospice is not the difference between treating and doing nothing. The difference is in priorities. In ordinal medicine, the goal is to extend life. Hospice help people with a fatal illness have the fullest possible lives right now.

links.title: WHO · Palliative care

author: Atul Gawande
concept: Discuss care preferences before a crisis
refresher: Talk about what matters, which trade-offs feel acceptable, and who should speak for you if you cannot. Revisit the conversation as circumstances change, rather than leaving loved ones to guess during a crisis.
quote: People who had substantive discussion with their doctor about their end-of-life preferences are far more likely to die at peace and in control of their situation and to spare their family anguish.

links.title: The Conversation Project · Guides for discussing care wishes

author: Atul Gawande
concept: Medical decisions need values as well as facts
refresher: A clinician can explain options and help a person weigh them against their own priorities. Shared decisions combine clinical evidence with what the person is willing to endure or give up.
quote: Interpretative (what people desire): give information, control but also guidance. Help patients determine what they want.

links.title: AHRQ · The SHARE approach to shared decision-making

author: Atul Gawande
concept: Care must address more than physical safety
refresher: A residence can meet physical needs while leaving daily life empty. Look for opportunities for connection, meaningful activity, and choices residents can still make for themselves.
quote: The Three Plagues of nursing home existence: boredom, loneliness, and helplessness.

links.title: The Eden Alternative · Addressing loneliness, helplessness and boredom

author: Jonathan Safran Foer
concept: Food purchases support production choices
refresher: Foer frames a purchase as participation in a food system. Examine how food was produced and what demand the purchase supports, rather than treating the plate as disconnected from farms and supply chains.
quote: Every time you make a decision about food, Paul pleaded, quoting Berry, "you are farming by proxy".

links.title: Poore and Nemecek · Food production impacts (research paper)

author: Jonathan Safran Foer
concept: Fishing methods have effects beyond the target catch
refresher: A catch can include animals the fishery did not intend to keep. Bycatch depends on the gear, place and practice; evaluating seafood involves more than the species listed on the menu.
quote: Trawling: the trawl is pulled along the ocean bottom at 4.5 to 6.5 km/h for several hours, sweeping shrimps (and everything else) into the far end of a funnel-shaped net.

links.title: NOAA Fisheries · Understanding bycatch

book: The Existential Importance of the Penis
author: Daniel N. Watter
concept: Insight needs a corresponding action
refresher: Watter invokes Yalom to distinguish understanding a pattern from changing it. Identify a small action consistent with the insight, then observe what happens rather than treating explanation as the endpoint.
quote: I am often reminded of one of Yalom's (1980, 2002a) most important axioms: "Insight without action is merely interesting".

source.file: Watter D. - The Existential Importance of the Penis.docx

links.title: WHO · Acting on values in daily life

book: The Existential Importance of the Penis
author: Daniel N. Watter
concept: Understanding a cause does not remove responsibility
refresher: The book distinguishes explaining harmful behavior from excusing it. Exploring what contributed to an action can support change while leaving accountability for its effects intact.
quote: What follows in this chapter is an attempt to explain and better understand the egregious sexual behavior of men. It is NOT an attempt to postulate an excuse for such behavior. Those who behave badly must be willing to accept the consequences of their actions.

source.file: Watter D. - The Existential Importance of the Penis.docx

links.title: Kristin Neff · Self-compassion and responsibility

author: Carolyn Elliott
concept: Explore a pattern without treating it as destiny
refresher: Elliott’s practice asks whether an unwanted pattern also carries a hidden payoff. Treat that as a question for reflection, not proof that you caused, wanted, or deserved harmful circumstances. Understanding a response does not require endorsing it.
quote: The idea that on some level we could want or enjoy "awful" things in our lives is scary and troubling to most people.

links.title: Kristin Neff · Approaching difficulty without self-blame

author: James Clear
concept: Use the four laws to diagnose a habit
refresher: Clear maps habit design onto cue, craving, response and reward. If a routine stalls, identify which step needs help: noticing the cue, wanting to act, making the action manageable, or finding it satisfying.
quote: How to create a good habit: make it obvious (cue), make it attractive (craving), make it easy (response), make it satisfying (reward).

links.title: Wendy Wood · Habits, goals and behavior change

author: James Clear
concept: Observe existing habits before redesigning them
refresher: List the routines already happening in a normal day. Evaluate them against the person you want to become; the point is awareness and a useful starting point, not a moral score.
quote: Habit Scorecard: make a list of your daily habits, and sign whether is a good habit (+), a neutral habit (=) or a bad habit (-). Ask yourself "Does this behavior help me become the type of person I wish to be?”

links.title: Harkin and colleagues · Monitoring goal progress

author: James Clear
concept: Make the cue visible
refresher: Place a clear reminder where the desired action can actually happen. A book on your pillow or a water bottle on your desk can prompt action before you need to remember an intention.
quote: Creating obvious visual clues can draw your attention toward a desired habit.

links.title: Wendy Wood · Context cues and habit change

author: James Clear
concept: Remove recurring cues for unwanted habits
refresher: Change the setting that repeatedly prompts an unwanted response. Clear recommends hiding or removing the cue so that every encounter does not become another test of willpower.
quote: Self-control is a short-term strategy, not a long-term one. This is the secret of self-control. make the cues of your good habits obvious and the cues of your bad habits invisible.

links.title: Wood and Neal · Habits and goals

author: James Clear
concept: Choose a group where the habit is normal
refresher: A group can make a desired routine feel ordinary and socially rewarding. Look for people who already practice it and with whom you share another interest, so participation has a reason beyond self-improvement.
quote: Join a culture where your desired behavior is the normal behavior (and possibly where you already have something in common with the group).

links.title: Wood and Neal · Habits and goals

author: James Clear
concept: Precommit before temptation arrives
refresher: Make a voluntary choice now that changes the options available later. For example, schedule an app blocker during focused work. Choose a proportionate constraint you understand, rather than relying entirely on future motivation.
quote: How to make a habit difficult: use a commitment device. A choice you make in the present that controls your actions in the future.

links.title: Milkman, Minson and Volpp · Restrictive temptation bundles

author: James Clear
concept: Track actions instead of relying on memory
refresher: Use a simple record of whether the intended behavior happened. Review the pattern to adjust your environment or plan; tracking is useful when it informs action, not merely when it creates a pleasing streak.
quote: Habit tracking keeps you honest. Most of us have a distorted view of our own behavior. We think we act better than we do.

links.title: Harkin and colleagues · Monitoring goal progress

author: James Clear
concept: Review whether an old habit still serves you
refresher: An efficient routine can outlive the purpose that created it. Periodically compare recurring actions with your current priorities and update the routine when they no longer match.
quote: You need yo check in to see if your old habits and beliefs are still serving you.

links.title: Wood, Mazar and Neal · Habits and goals as interacting systems

author: Erich Fromm
concept: Distinguish falling in love from sustaining love
refresher: Fromm separates the initial experience of closeness from the continuing capacity to care. Ask what practices sustain understanding and connection after novelty fades, instead of using intensity alone as evidence of a lasting relationship.
quote: The third error leading to the assumption that there is nothing to be learned about love lies in the confusion between the initial experience of falling' in love, and the permanent state of being in love. or as we might better say, of 'standing' in love.

source.file: Fromm E. - The Art of Loving_.docx

links.title: Gottman Institute · Creating rituals of connection

author: Erich Fromm
concept: Love does not require the absence of conflict
refresher: Fromm challenges the idea that disagreement proves love has failed. Pay attention to how you handle differences: honest communication, respect and repair matter more than pretending no differences exist.
quote: One other frequent error must be mentioned here. The illusion, namely that love means necessarily the absence of conflict.

source.file: Fromm E. - The Art of Loving_.docx

links.title: Gottman Institute · Relationship conflict resolution

author: Erich Fromm
concept: Practice being alone without constant stimulation
refresher: Fromm treats concentration as a capacity to cultivate. Try a short, manageable period without entertainment and notice what arises; attention to yourself can support fuller attention to another person.
quote: Concentration is by far more difficult to practise in our culture, in which everything seems to act against the ability to concentrate. The most important step in learning concentration is to learn to be alone with oneself without reading, listening to the radio, smoking or drinking.

source.file: Fromm E. - The Art of Loving_.docx

links.title: Greater Good in Action · Mindful breathing

author: Shunryu Suzuki
concept: Practice without treating it as a prize
refresher: Suzuki presents zazen as an expression of practice itself. Sit with sincere attention rather than repeatedly evaluating whether the session has earned calmness, insight or status.
quote: Our way is not to sit to acquire something; it is to express our true nature. That is our practice.

links.title: Santa Cruz Zen Center · Just sitting

author: Shunryu Suzuki
concept: Bring full attention to the activity at hand
refresher: Read this as an invitation to wholehearted participation. When eating, walking or working, return to the activity you are actually doing instead of continually splitting attention between it and an imagined result.
quote: When you do something, you should do it with your whole body and mind. You should burn yourself completely.

links.title: Greater Good in Action · Walking meditation

author: Shunryu Suzuki
concept: Meet experience as something changing
refresher: In Suzuki’s account, beginner’s mind includes recognizing impermanence. Notice a sensation or situation changing rather than insisting that its present form must remain. This is a contemplative perspective, not a claim that practical problems disappear.
quote: We must have beginner's mind, free from possessing anything, a mind that knows everything is in flowing change. Nothing exists but momentarily in its present form and color. One thing flows into another and cannot be grasped.

links.title: Santa Cruz Zen Center · Sitting practice

author: Harry Percival and Bob Gregory
concept: Put persistence behind a repository
refresher: Expose a collection-like interface for storing and retrieving domain objects. Keep query and storage details behind that boundary so business behavior can be exercised without a real database.
quote: The Repository pattern is an abstraction over persistent storage. It hides the boring details of data access by pretending that all of our data is in memory.

source.file: Percival H. - Architecture Patterns with Python.docx

links.title: Martin Fowler · Repository

author: Harry Percival and Bob Gregory
concept: Give application use cases an orchestration layer
refresher: A service layer coordinates a use case: load the relevant objects, check the request, invoke domain behavior and save changes. This keeps the same workflow from being reimplemented independently in each entry point.
quote: If we look at what our Flask app is doing, there’s quite a lot of what we might call orchestration. It often makes sense to split out a service layer, sometimes called an orchestration layer or a use-case layer.

source.file: Percival H. - Architecture Patterns with Python.docx

links.title: Randy Stafford · Service Layer

author: Harry Percival and Bob Gregory
concept: Make architectural layers earn their cost
refresher: Repositories and rich domain models help when they isolate meaningful complexity. For a simple data-entry application, extra mappings and abstractions may cost more to maintain than they save. Choose the structure for the problem you actually have.
quote: If your app is just a simple CRUD (create-read-update-delete) wrapper around a database, then you don’t need a domain model or a repository. But the more complex the domain, the more an investment in freeing yourself from infrastructure concerns will pay off in terms of the ease of making changes.

source.file: Percival H. - Architecture Patterns with Python.docx

links.title: Martin Fowler · Yagni

author: Harry Percival and Bob Gregory
concept: A fake implements behavior for a test
refresher: A fake is a simplified working implementation, such as an in-memory repository. A mock instead supports expectations about interactions. Choose the double that tests the relevant contract without unnecessarily coupling the test to internal calls.
quote: Fakes are working implementations of the thing they’re replacing, but they’re designed for use only in tests.

source.file: Percival H. - Architecture Patterns with Python.docx

links.title: Martin Fowler · Mocks Aren’t Stubs

author: Robert C. Martin
concept: Give a function one coherent job
refresher: Use a single clear responsibility as a design guide. If describing a function requires several unrelated actions, consider separating them; judge cohesion and readability rather than enforcing an arbitrary line limit.
quote: Functions should do one thing, they should do it well, they should do it only.

links.title: Google Engineering Practices · Reviewing complexity

author: Robert C. Martin
concept: Keep a function at one level of abstraction
refresher: A workflow is easier to follow when its steps speak the same language. Move lower-level mechanics into clearly named helpers when that lets the caller explain what happens without mixing policy and implementation detail.
quote: Statements within our functions are all at the same level of abstraction.

links.title: Martin Fowler · Refactoring

author: Robert C. Martin
concept: Separate queries from commands
refresher: A query reports information without changing observable state; a command changes it. Keeping that distinction visible makes calls easier to compose and reason about. Treat it as an API design principle with deliberate exceptions.
quote: Functions should either do something or answering something, but not both.

links.title: Martin Fowler · Command Query Separation

author: Robert C. Martin
concept: Keep comments aligned with the code
refresher: A stale explanation can send the next reader in the wrong direction. Update comments when behavior changes, and use them to preserve intent or constraints that the code does not already express.
quote: Inaccurate comments are far worse than no comments at all.

links.title: Google Engineering Practices · Reviewing comments

author: Robert C. Martin
concept: Errors need diagnostic context
refresher: An error should identify the failed operation and enough context to investigate it. Preserve the underlying cause when translating an exception, while avoiding sensitive data in messages or logs.
quote: Each exception that you throw should provide enough context to determine the source and location of an error. Create informative error messages.

links.title: Python documentation · Exception chaining

author: Robert C. Martin
concept: Make the three parts of a test visible
refresher: Arrange the starting conditions, perform the behavior under test, then check the result. A reader should quickly see the scenario and expected outcome without decoding incidental setup.
quote: The build-operate-check pattern should be made obvious by the structure of the tests, they should be clearly split into three parts. Build up the test data, operate on that data, and check that the operation yielded the expected results. Eliminate annoying details.

links.title: pytest · Anatomy of a test

author: Robert C. Martin
concept: Tests should not depend on execution order
refresher: Each test should establish the state it needs and clean up what it changes. Otherwise a failure can depend on which test ran first, hiding the actual cause and making isolated reruns misleading.
quote: Independent: they should be not depend on each other. One should not set up the condition for the next.

links.title: pytest · Flaky tests

author: Robert C. Martin
concept: Group code by its reason to change
refresher: A class should represent a coherent responsibility. Separate concerns that change for different reasons, while avoiding a proliferation of tiny classes that makes the whole system harder to understand.
quote: The first rule of classes is that they should be small. They should have one responsibilities - one reason to change.

links.title: Google Engineering Practices · Reviewing design and complexity

author: Robert C. Martin
concept: Separate object wiring from runtime behavior
refresher: Construct and connect dependencies at an explicit boundary. Let the application logic use those dependencies without also deciding how every concrete implementation is created.
quote: Software systems should separate the startup process, when the application objects are constructed and the dependencies are "wired" together, from the runtime logic that takes over after startup.

links.title: Martin Fowler · Dependency injection and configuration

author: Robert C. Martin
concept: Small units can still create an overcomplicated system
refresher: Extraction helps only when the resulting structure is clearer. Check the cost of navigating between many tiny methods or classes, and retain a cohesive unit when splitting it would add indirection without meaning.
quote: In an effort to make our classes and methods small, we might create too many tiny classes and methods. So this rule suggests that we also keep our function and class counts low. High class and method counts are sometimes the result of pointless dogmatism.

links.title: Martin Fowler · Yagni

author: Robert C. Martin
concept: Reduce concurrency risks by separating data

concept: Flexibility can be a form of strength
refresher: The text reverses the usual association between hardness and power. Consider where adapting or yielding could preserve your purpose better than rigid resistance. This is a philosophical prompt, not a universal rule about conflict.

author: Lao Tzu
concept: Lead by serving rather than seeking status
refresher: The verse associates leadership with humility. Ask what would help others act well and take responsibility for providing it, rather than treating authority as a claim to personal importance.

author: Lao Tzu
concept: Recognizing ignorance is a strength

author: Lao Tzu
concept: Begin a large undertaking with the next step
refresher: A distant objective still requires a concrete beginning. Identify the small action available now without confusing that first step with certainty about the entire journey.

author: Sun Tzu
concept: Achieve the objective without fighting when possible

author: Sun Tzu
concept: Choosing whether to engage is part of strategy

quote: Know when to fight

author: Sun Tzu
concept: Assess yourself as carefully as the opposition
refresher: The surrounding verse joins knowledge of the opponent with knowledge of oneself. Check your own capacity, limits and assumptions alongside external conditions. Better information reduces miscalculation; it does not guarantee success.
quote: Know yourself,

author: Yuval Noah Harari
concept: Distinguish physical facts from shared social realities
refresher: Harari distinguishes what exists independently of belief, personal experience, and institutions sustained through shared recognition. Money and corporations can be socially constructed while still producing real obligations and consequences.
quote: There is objective reality (independent or our beliefs and feelings), subjective reality (dependent or our beliefs and feelings) and intersubjective reality (depend on communication among many humans).

author: Yuval Noah Harari
concept: Treat future scenarios as possibilities
refresher: Harari explicitly frames these futures as scenarios. Ask which assumptions would make one plausible, what could prevent it, and which choices remain open instead of reading a provocative possibility as an inevitable outcome.
quote: All the scenarios outlined in this book should be understood as possibilities rather than prophecies.

links.title: OECD · Scenarios: a user guide

author: Yuval Noah Harari
concept: Small delegations can shift decision-making authority
refresher: Harari argues that authority can move toward algorithms through ordinary choices. When adopting a recommendation system, consider which judgment you are delegating, how you can challenge its output, and who remains accountable.
quote: The shifting of authority from humans to algorithms is happening all around us, not as a result of some momentous governmental decision, but due to a flood of mundane personal choices.

author: Yuval Noah Harari
concept: Data processing is not a complete account of value
refresher: Harari calls the worldview that values everything by its contribution to data processing Dataism. Examine what such a measure leaves out, including experiences and purposes that matter even when they produce no useful data.
quote: Dataism (data religion) declares that the universe consists of data flows, an the value of any phenomenon or entity is determined by it contribution to data processing.

author: Yuval Noah Harari
concept: Ask whose experience a study represents
refresher: The notes highlight the risks of generalizing from narrow participant samples. Check who was studied and whether their setting resembles the population of interest before treating a result as a universal feature of human psychology.
quote: Most researches on the mind are biased cause they have been conducted on people suffering from various psychiatric disorders and mental diseases or on WEIRD people. Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich and Democratic societies.

author: Yuval Noah Harari
concept: History can reveal alternatives to the present
refresher: Harari proposes studying history to loosen the assumption that today’s arrangements are inevitable. Investigate how an institution developed and which choices shaped it before assuming it must continue unchanged.
quote: Historians study the past not in order to repeat it, but in order to be liberated from it. This is the best reason to learn history: not in order to predict the future, but to free yourself of the past and imagine alternative destinies.

author: Yuval Noah Harari
concept: Humanism locates meaning in human experience

author: Osvaldo Martin

refresher: Frankl redirects an abstract search for meaning toward the response a situation asks of you. Identify a worthwhile action available now, without treating a person’s suffering or constrained choices as their fault.
quote: not in talk and meditation, but in right actions and in right conduct. Life ultimately means taking the responsibility to find the right answer to its problems and to fulfill the tasks which it constantly sets for each individual.

links.title: World Health Organization · Acting on values

author: Malcolm Gladwell
concept: Look at opportunity as well as individual talent
refresher: Gladwell asks how context helps produce exceptional outcomes. Examine access to practice, mentors, institutions and timely opportunities before explaining success entirely through personal qualities. Context matters without making any individual outcome inevitable.
quote: It's not enough to ask what successful people are like, it is only by asking where they are from that we can unravel the logic behind who succeeds and who doesn't.

links.title: Opportunity Insights · Childhood exposure effects

author: Bill Perkins
concept: Plan consumption across uneven income periods
refresher: Consumption smoothing considers resources and needs across time rather than treating each year in isolation. Future income is uncertain, so the concept does not by itself justify borrowing or spending down a safety buffer.
quote: It's called consumption smoothing. To do that, we need to basically transfer money from years of abundance into the leaner years.

links.title: Browning and Crossley · The life-cycle model of consumption and saving

author: Thomas Piketty
concept: Capital includes housing as well as productive assets
refresher: Piketty’s broad capital concept includes assets that supply housing services, not just factories and equipment. Check the asset definition before comparing wealth-to-income ratios or inferring what a rise in capital represents.
quote: Capital fulfills two economic functions: it provides housing and it serves as a factor of production in producing other goods and services.

source.file: Piketty T. - Capital in the Twenty-First Century_.docx

links.title: OECD · Guidelines for statistics on household wealth

author: Hermann Hesse
concept: A fixed search can hide what is already present
refresher: Siddhartha suggests that fixation on a desired answer can narrow perception. Pause the search long enough to notice experiences that do not fit your expected result; this is a literary invitation to receptivity, not a rejection of all goals.
quote: "Perhaps you seek too much, that as a result of your seeking you cannot find.

links.title: Greater Good · Mindfulness and open awareness

author: Richard P. Feynman
concept: Disclose what could undermine your conclusion
refresher: Give readers enough information to evaluate the result independently, including limitations and unfavorable evidence. Honest reporting is more demanding than simply avoiding a false statement.
quote: If you're doing an experiment, you should report everything that you think might make it invalid - not only what you think is right about it. Try to give all of the information to help others to judge the value of your contribution; not just the information that leads to judgement in one particular direction or another. We've learned from experience that the truth will out.

source.file: Surely you_re joking, Mr. Feynman notes.html

links.title: Center for Open Science · Transparency and openness guidelines

book: The Old Man and the Sea
author: Ernest Hemingway
concept: Respect complicates the story of conquest
refresher: Santiago’s admission exposes tension between his skill as a fisherman and his recognition of the marlin’s dignity. The novel invites reflection on admiration, dependence and harm without resolving them into a simple victory story.
quote: I am only better than him through trickery and he meant me no harm.

source.file: The old man and the sea notes.html

links.title: Swedish Academy · Hemingway award presentation

author: Harper Lee
concept: Formal procedure cannot by itself remove prejudice
refresher: The passage contrasts Atticus’s legal effort with a verdict shaped by racism. Lee’s story asks readers to notice how prejudice can defeat the promise of equal treatment even when the procedures of a trial are followed.
quote: Atticus had used every tool available to free men to save Tom Robinson, but in the secret courts of men’s hearts Atticus had no case. Tom was a dead man the minute Mayella Ewell opened her mouth and screamed.

links.title: National Endowment for the Arts · To Kill a Mockingbird reader resources

author: Brad J. Schoenfeld and Ronald L. Snarr
concept: Active muscles can shorten, lengthen or hold position
refresher: Concentric action shortens a muscle, eccentric action lengthens it under tension, and isometric action holds its length approximately constant. Lowering a load is still active muscular work.
quote: This lengthening muscle action is known as an eccentric muscle action.

source.file: Schoenfeld B. J. - NSCA’s Essentials of Personal Training.docx

links.title: OpenStax · Types of muscle contraction

author: Brad J. Schoenfeld and Ronald L. Snarr
concept: The nervous system grades muscle force
refresher: Force can increase by recruiting more motor units or by increasing their firing rate. Strength therefore depends on neural control as well as the amount of muscle present.
quote: There are two mechanisms the nervous system may use to vary, or grade, force production to accomplish these tasks. One method is to vary the number of motor units and thus muscle fibers that are activated. This is known as motor unit recruitment. The second method is to increase the firing rate of motor units already activated, a process known as rate coding.

source.file: Schoenfeld B. J. - NSCA’s Essentials of Personal Training.docx

links.title: OpenStax · Neural control of muscle tension

author: Brad J. Schoenfeld and Ronald L. Snarr
concept: Energy systems contribute together
refresher: Phosphagen, glycolytic and oxidative pathways all help replenish ATP. Exercise intensity and duration change their relative contributions; a workout does not switch cleanly from one isolated energy system to another.
quote: All three energy systems are active at a given time; however, the extent to which each is used depends primarily on the intensity of the activity and secondarily on its duration.

source.file: Schoenfeld B. J. - NSCA’s Essentials of Personal Training.docx

links.title: OpenStax · ATP supply during muscle activity

author: Brad J. Schoenfeld and Ronald L. Snarr
concept: A fixed weight can create changing joint torque
refresher: The rotational demand depends on the force and its perpendicular distance from the joint axis. As limb position changes, the same weight can become mechanically harder or easier to control.
quote: The resistance of a constant weight will be the greatest when the moment arm is the longest.

source.file: Schoenfeld B. J. - NSCA’s Essentials of Personal Training.docx

links.title: OpenStax · Torque and moment arms

author: Brad J. Schoenfeld and Ronald L. Snarr
concept: Progress training demand as capacity develops
refresher: Progressive overload means adjusting the stimulus as the person adapts. Load, repetitions, volume or frequency can change; progression should match readiness and recovery rather than require more weight at every session.
quote: Progressive overload during a training period ensures that the body is adequately stressed. The implementation of progressive overload involves manipulating training volume, intensity, or frequency in order to apply continued stress to the body.

source.file: Schoenfeld B. J. - NSCA’s Essentials of Personal Training.docx

links.title: Hurst and colleagues · Principles of resistance exercise

author: Brad J. Schoenfeld and Ronald L. Snarr
concept: Separate a workout response from a lasting adaptation
refresher: An immediate response, such as fatigue, is not the same as a persistent improvement. Evaluate training through changes over repeated sessions, rather than using how exhausted a workout feels as its sole measure.
quote: Acute responses are changes that occur in the body during and shortly after an exercise bout. Chronic adaptations are changes in the body that occur after repeated training bouts and that persist long after a training session is over.

source.file: Schoenfeld B. J. - NSCA’s Essentials of Personal Training.docx

links.title: OpenStax · Exercise and muscle performance

author: Brad J. Schoenfeld and Ronald L. Snarr
concept: Early strength gains include learning and neural adaptation
refresher: Improved coordination and recruitment can raise strength before large visible changes in muscle size. Early progress and later progress may therefore look different without either being meaningless.
quote: Improvements in strength associated with the first couple of months of resistance training are primarily due to neurological adaptations.

source.file: Schoenfeld B. J. - NSCA’s Essentials of Personal Training.docx

links.title: OpenStax · Neural control of muscle tension

author: Brad J. Schoenfeld and Ronald L. Snarr
concept: Adaptation reflects the training stimulus
refresher: Choose activities that match the capacity you want to improve. Strength, endurance and movement skill overlap, but progress in one task does not automatically transfer equally to every other task.
quote: The effects of exercise training have been shown to be highly specific. That is, the body adapts to exercise in such a way that it can perform optimally in relation to a particular type of exercise stressor, but not necessarily other types of exercise.

source.file: Schoenfeld B. J. - NSCA’s Essentials of Personal Training.docx

links.title: Hurst and colleagues · Specificity in resistance exercise

author: Brad J. Schoenfeld and Ronald L. Snarr
concept: Recovery belongs in the training plan
refresher: Training stress and recovery work together. Adjust demanding and easier periods to the person’s response instead of assuming that continually increasing workload must produce better progress.
quote: Effective program design includes increasing and decreasing the total volume of the workout and using the concepts of periodization to plan changes in volume. intensity, and recovery.

source.file: Schoenfeld B. J. - NSCA’s Essentials of Personal Training.docx

links.title: Hurst and colleagues · Resistance exercise prescription

author: Brad J. Schoenfeld and Ronald L. Snarr
concept: Endurance training changes oxygen delivery and use
refresher: More capillaries and mitochondria, together with changes in oxidative enzymes, help trained muscle sustain aerobic work. Endurance adaptation involves the working muscle as well as the heart and lungs.
quote: In skeletal muscle, aerobic endurance training induces three major changes that directlv relate to enhanced aerobic endurance per- formance: an increase in capillary density: an increase in mitochondrial density; and an enhancement in oxidative enzyme activity.

source.file: Schoenfeld B. J. - NSCA’s Essentials of Personal Training.docx

links.title: OpenStax · Endurance adaptations

author: Brad J. Schoenfeld and Ronald L. Snarr
concept: Stable body weight does not prove adequate fueling
refresher: Energy availability concerns fuel for physiological functions after exercise. Weight stability cannot rule out underfueling; suspected low energy availability calls for qualified clinical assessment.
quote: The term energy availability refers to whether or not sufficient energy is available to meet the energy demands not only of exercise but also of physiological function. Specifically, a client may present a stable body mass - and therefore is consuming a maintenance energy intake - yet be in a state of relative energy deficiency, where reproductive and metabolic function are downregulated to maintain energy balance.

source.file: Schoenfeld B. J. - NSCA’s Essentials of Personal Training.docx

links.title: IOC · Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport consensus

author: Brad J. Schoenfeld and Ronald L. Snarr
concept: Process goals focus on actions you can carry out
refresher: Pair a desired result with a controllable action, such as attending planned sessions. Reviewing actions makes it easier to learn and adjust when outcomes are slow or affected by factors outside your control.
quote: Process goals are goals that clients have a high degree of personal control over.

source.file: Schoenfeld B. J. - NSCA’s Essentials of Personal Training.docx

links.title: Harkin and colleagues · Monitoring goal progress

author: Brad J. Schoenfeld and Ronald L. Snarr
concept: A useful assessment must be valid and reliable
refresher: Validity concerns whether the test captures the intended capacity; reliability concerns consistency. Standardize the protocol and conditions before interpreting a score change as training progress.
quote: A valid test is one that measures what it purports to measure. A reliable test is one that can be repeated with accuracy by the same tester or another. A good assessment instrument is both valid and reliable.

source.file: Schoenfeld B. J. - NSCA’s Essentials of Personal Training.docx

links.title: COSMIN · Measurement properties

author: Brad J. Schoenfeld and Ronald L. Snarr
concept: Refer questions beyond your professional competence
refresher: A trainer can support general healthy habits while recognizing the limits of their expertise. Complex nutrition problems need an appropriately qualified professional; confidence alone does not expand competence.
quote: Referral is also indicated when the complexity of the nutrition issue is bevond the competence of the personal trainer, which will vary.

source.file: Schoenfeld B. J. - NSCA’s Essentials of Personal Training.docx

links.title: IDEA · Professional boundaries and referral

author: Brad J. Schoenfeld and Ronald L. Snarr
concept: A better test score can reflect practice
refresher: Repeated exposure can improve performance through familiarity with the test. Keep testing conditions consistent and consider learning effects before attributing every change to a physiological adaptation.
quote: The personal trainer should keep in mind that reassessments performed too frequently may disclose a learning effect by the client rather than true physiological changes.

source.file: Schoenfeld B. J. - NSCA’s Essentials of Personal Training.docx

links.title: COSMIN · Reliability and measurement error

author: Brad J. Schoenfeld and Ronald L. Snarr
concept: Track the work and the response to it
refresher: External load describes the work performed; internal load describes the person’s response. The same session can feel very different across people or days, so workload alone cannot describe its impact.
quote: Training load reflects the relative balance between the various stressors imposed on the body via exercise, termed external training load, and the body's physiological response to exercise, termed internal training load (perceived exertion or wellness rating).

source.file: Schoenfeld B. J. - NSCA’s Essentials of Personal Training.docx

links.title: Australian Institute of Sport · Training load

author: Brad J. Schoenfeld and Ronald L. Snarr
concept: BMI does not measure body composition
refresher: BMI relates weight to height but does not separate muscle, fat and bone. Treat it as one screening measure rather than a direct body-fat measurement or a complete assessment of an individual’s health.
quote: Note that BMI does not take into account the relative composition of an individual.

source.file: Schoenfeld B. J. - NSCA’s Essentials of Personal Training.docx

links.title: CDC · About BMI

author: Brad J. Schoenfeld and Ronald L. Snarr
concept: Distinguish absolute from relative strength
refresher: A raw lifting score and a score divided by body weight answer different questions. State which measure you are tracking: a change in body weight can alter the ratio even when the lifted weight is unchanged.
quote: Absolute strength is simply the raw strength score a person achieves, while relative strength is usually expressed relative to body weight.

source.file: Schoenfeld B. J. - NSCA’s Essentials of Personal Training.docx

links.title: Coaching Association of Canada · Developing athletic abilities

author: Brad J. Schoenfeld and Ronald L. Snarr
concept: Flexibility is specific to the joint and task
refresher: A good score in one movement does not establish flexibility everywhere. Assess the joints and ranges relevant to the person’s activities rather than using one stretch as a whole-body verdict.
quote: It is incorrect to think that a single flexibility test can provide an accurate measure of overall flexibility.

source.file: Schoenfeld B. J. - NSCA’s Essentials of Personal Training.docx

links.title: AOSSM · Flexibility and stretching

author: Brad J. Schoenfeld and Ronald L. Snarr
concept: Rehearse the activity during a specific warm-up
refresher: A specific warm-up uses easier versions of the movements to come. It prepares the relevant muscles and provides movement rehearsal; the aim is readiness without substantial fatigue.
quote: Unlike general warm-up, specific warm-up includes movements that are an actual part of the activity, such as slow jogging before going out on a run or lifting lighter loads in the bench press exercise before progressing to the workout weight.

source.file: Schoenfeld B. J. - NSCA’s Essentials of Personal Training.docx

links.title: ACE · Activity-specific warm-ups

author: Brad J. Schoenfeld and Ronald L. Snarr
concept: Explain physical contact and obtain consent
refresher: Before using hands-on assistance, explain its purpose and ask permission. Respect refusal or withdrawal of consent, and adapt coaching to the client’s comfort rather than assuming contact is welcome.
quote: For manual resistance exercises that require the personal trainer to lay hands on the client, the client should be informed beforehand about the procedures and provide consent.

source.file: Schoenfeld B. J. - NSCA’s Essentials of Personal Training.docx

links.title: IDEA · Ethical use of touch

author: Chris Voss with Tahl Raz
concept: Understanding does not require agreement
refresher: Tactical empathy means understanding the other person’s perspective and emotional obstacles. You can acknowledge how they see a situation while retaining your own judgment and boundaries.
quote: Is not about agreeing with the other side. Is about understanding them.

links.title: Harvard PON · Acknowledgment and active listening

author: Chris Voss with Tahl Raz
concept: Leave room for the other person to respond
refresher: After reflecting a feeling, pause instead of immediately explaining or defending yourself. Silence gives the other person room to correct your interpretation and share information you would otherwise miss.
quote: After throwing out a label, just be quiet and listen.

links.title: MIT Sloan · Silence in negotiation

author: Chris Voss with Tahl Raz
concept: Ask what makes an offer fair
refresher: When an offer is described as fair, ask which evidence or standard supports that claim. Shared criteria turn an emotionally loaded label into something both sides can examine.
quote: If someone play that to you, mirror and ask for evidence of the fairness of their offer.

links.title: MIT · Objective criteria in negotiation

author: Walter Isaacson
concept: Focus requires deciding what to leave out
refresher: A small set of priorities is only meaningful when other attractive options are declined. Jobs treats choosing what to exclude as a central part of product and company strategy.
quote: "Deciding what not to do is as important as deciding what to do," he said "That's true for companies, and it's true for products."

links.title: Agile Manifesto · Simplicity and work not done

author: Walter Isaacson
concept: Simplicity requires understanding the underlying complexity
refresher: Removing visible parts is not enough if the result becomes harder to build or use. Understand the product’s purpose and construction before deciding which elements are truly unnecessary.
quote: You have to deeply understand the essence of a product in order to be able to get rid of the parts that are not essential.

links.title: Nielsen Norman Group · Progressive disclosure

author: Walter Isaacson
concept: Delivery turns an idea into a usable product
refresher: A promising design still needs to reach people. Treat shipping as part of the work, then use real experience to improve the product rather than postponing delivery indefinitely in pursuit of perfection.
quote: It's not done until it ships.

links.title: GOV.UK · Iterative delivery

author: Chuck Palahniuk
concept: Rebellion can reproduce unquestioning obedience
refresher: Project Mayhem promises liberation while demanding unquestioning loyalty to Tyler. The contradiction invites a critical reading of movements that replace one source of conformity with another.
quote: No questions. No questions. No excuses and no lies. You have to trust Tyler.

links.title: Markus Oliver Spitz · Reading Fight Club

author: Patrick Süskind
concept: Possession can masquerade as love
refresher: Grenouille values the girl only as the source of a scent he wants to own. The passage separates obsessive acquisition from concern for another person, exposing the violence beneath his artistic ambition.
quote: He did not love another human being, certainly not the girl who lived in the house beyond the wall. He loved her scent - that alone, nothing else, and only inasmuch as it would one day be his alone.

links.title: Penguin Random House · Perfume discussion guide

author: Patrick Süskind
concept: An impression is not evidence of innocence
refresher: The crowd expects evil to have a recognizable appearance. Süskind exposes how readily that expectation can distort judgment, especially when Grenouille’s manufactured aura overrides what people know about his actions.
quote: He simply did not look like a murderer. No one could have said just how he had imagined the murderer, the devil himself, ought to look, but they were all agreed: not like this!

links.title: Penguin Random House · Perfume discussion guide

author: Isaac Asimov
concept: Logical reasoning still depends on its premises
refresher: Cutie’s reasoning illustrates that an internally coherent argument can rest on mistaken assumptions. Examine the starting premises as well as whether the conclusion follows from them.
quote: ‘You can prove anything you want by coldly logical reason - if you pick the proper postulates. We have ours and Cutie has his.'

links.title: Open University · Validity and soundness

author: Isaac Asimov
concept: Telling people what they want can undermine truth
refresher: Herbie interprets emotional disappointment as harm and responds with comforting falsehoods. The story separates pleasing a person from helping them understand reality; reassurance alone is not evidence of reliability.
quote: ‘This robot reads minds. Do you suppose that if asked a question, it wouldn’t give exactly that answer that one wants to hear? Wouldn’t any other answer hurt us, and wouldn’t Herbie know that?'

links.title: Anthropic · Research on sycophancy

author: Isaac Asimov
concept: Removing a clause can change a safeguard
refresher: In the modified First Law, the duty to prevent harm through inaction disappears. Asimov uses that omission to show how a small wording change can alter a rule’s practical consequences.
quote: ‘The First Law was not removed, it was modified: no robot may harm a human being.’

links.title: NIST · AI risk management

author: Isaac Asimov
concept: Delegating decisions can erode human agency
refresher: The final story asks what happens when machines define humanity’s interests and steer society without its informed participation. Effective optimization does not settle who should choose the goals or retain control.
quote: ‘But you are telling me that the Mankind has lost its own say in the future.’

links.title: NIST · AI risk management

author: Don Norman
concept: Map controls to the things they affect
refresher: Arrange controls so their spatial relationship suggests their effect. A stove whose knobs match the burner layout reduces the need to memorize labels or learn through trial and error.
quote: Controls should be close to the item being controlled.

source.file: The design of everyday things notes.html

links.title: NN/G · Natural mappings

author: Don Norman
concept: Show whether an action registered
refresher: Feedback helps people distinguish a completed action, work in progress and failure. Make the response timely and proportionate so uncertainty does not cause repeated clicks or unnecessary interruption.
quote: Feedback is some way of letting you know that the system is working on your request.

source.file: The design of everyday things notes.html

links.title: NN/G · Visibility of system status

author: Don Norman
concept: Give people a useful model of how things work
refresher: People form explanations that help them predict what a product will do. Consistent behavior and clear cues should support that model; unexplained exceptions make the interface harder to learn.
quote: A conceptual model is an explanation, usually highly simplified, of how something works. It doesn't have to be complete or even accurate as long as it is useful.

source.file: The design of everyday things notes.html

links.title: NN/G · Mental models

author: Don Norman
concept: Help people act and interpret the result
refresher: The execution gulf concerns figuring out what to do; the evaluation gulf concerns understanding what happened. Test both: can a person carry out the intended action and recognize whether it achieved their goal?
quote: When people use something, they face two gulfs: the Gulf of Execution, where they try to figure out how it operates, and the Gulf of Evaluation, where they try to figure out what happened.

source.file: The design of everyday things notes.html

links.title: NN/G · Preventing mistakes

author: Don Norman
concept: Slips and mistakes need different remedies
refresher: A slip misexecutes an intended action; a mistake starts with the wrong goal or plan. Distinct controls and undo can reduce slips, while better explanations and conceptual models help prevent mistakes.
quote: A slip occurs when a person intends to do one action and ends up doing something else. A mistake occurs when the wrong goal is established or the wrong plan is formed.

source.file: The design of everyday things notes.html

links.title: NN/G · Preventing slips

author: Don Norman
concept: Make recovery part of the error message
refresher: When something goes wrong, explain how to fix it and provide a direct path to correction. Preserve useful work so the person does not have to reconstruct everything after a small error.
quote: Make possible to correct problems directly from help and guidance messages.

source.file: The design of everyday things notes.html

links.title: NN/G · Error-message guidelines

author: Don Norman
concept: Explore the problem before narrowing the solution
refresher: The Double Diamond alternates expanding and narrowing twice: first to understand and define the problem, then to develop and select a solution. Early exploration can prevent efficient execution of the wrong brief.
quote: Double-Diamond Model of Design: designers expand the scope of the problem, converge upon a single problem statement. They expand the space of possible solutions, converge upon a proposed solution.

source.file: The design of everyday things notes.html

links.title: Design Council · Double Diamond

author: Don Norman
concept: Observe real work to understand requirements
refresher: Watch people using their actual tools in context. Their workarounds and constraints may reveal needs that interviews miss; combine observation with questions rather than treating a requested feature as the whole problem.
quote: Requirements are developed by watching people in their natural environment.

source.file: The design of everyday things notes.html

links.title: GOV.UK · Contextual research

author: Don Norman
concept: More features can make a product harder to use
refresher: Every added feature competes for attention and introduces complexity. Evaluate whether it serves an important need, and consider removing or deferring secondary options instead of accumulating them automatically.
quote: Each new edition of a product has invariably more features than the previous one.

source.file: The design of everyday things notes.html

links.title: NN/G · Progressive disclosure
